verses.text: David consulted with the captains of thousands and of hundreds, even with every leader.

David said to all the assembly of Israel, “If it seems good to you, and if it is of Yahweh our God, let us send word everywhere to our brothers who are left in all the land of Israel, with whom the priests and Levites are in their cities that have suburbs, that they may gather themselves to us.
Also, let us again bring the ark of our God back to us; for we didn’t seek it in the days of Saul.”
All the assembly said that they would do so; for the thing was right in the eyes of all the people.
So David assembled all Israel together, from the Shihor the brook of Egypt even to the entrance of Hamath, to bring God’s ark from Kiriath Jearim.
David went up with all Israel to Baalah, that is, to Kiriath Jearim, which belonged to Judah, to bring up from there God Yahweh’s ark that sits above the cherubim, that is called by the Name.
They carried God’s ark on a new cart, and brought it out of Abinadab’s house; and Uzza and Ahio drove the cart.
David and all Israel played before God with all their might, even with songs, with harps, with stringed instruments, with tambourines, with cymbals, and with trumpets.
When they came to Chidon’s threshing floor, Uzza put out his hand to hold the ark; for the oxen stumbled.
Yahweh’s anger burned against Uzza, and he struck him, because he put his hand on the ark; and he died there before God.
David was displeased, because Yahweh had broken out against Uzza. He called that place Perez Uzza, to this day.
David was afraid of God that day, saying, “How can I bring God’s ark home to me?”
So David didn’t move the ark with him into David’s city, but carried it aside into Obed-Edom the Gittite’s house.
God’s ark remained with the family of Obed-Edom in his house three months; and Yahweh blessed Obed-Edom’s house and all that he had.

footnotes.content: David didn't act alone—he first gathered the leaders, the heads of thousands and hundreds, to hear them. This is a picture of wisdom seeking counsel, a king who knows his strength lies not in himself but in the minds and hearts of those around him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Notice David's speech: 'If it seems good to you, and if it is of the Lord our God.' He puts the decision before both the people and the Almighty, not commanding but inviting. Even a king's will must bow first to God's will and his people's voice.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The ark had been neglected in Saul's reign—forty years without the throne of God's presence actively sought in Israel's worship. David sees this absence as a wound to heal, a holy thing left in exile that must be brought home.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Unanimity: 'All the assembly said they would do so; for the thing was right in the eyes of all.' When a desire aligns with God's will and wins the hearts of the people, there is no resistance—only readiness and joy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David gathered 'all Israel' from Shihor (Egypt's border) to Hamath (the north)—the entire land united in one mission. This massive mobilization shows how the ark's retrieval was not a private gesture but a matter of national restoration.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Kiriath Jearim—the ark had sat there for decades, a place on Judah's hills where the holy was kept safe but removed, 'called by the Name' but not yet crowned in its proper place. David's journey to retrieve it is a journey of longing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A new cart, not one consecrated for this sacred task. Already a choice is being made—the method, not the heart, is the problem. The ark requires the old way, the Levitical way, though no one yet sees the danger.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Music, singing, harps, cymbals, trumpets—a joy-filled procession that shows David's love for the Lord. The joy is genuine and earnest. Yet joyful intent and correct method are not the same thing, and God tests the difference.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Chidon's threshing floor—a mundane place where sudden holiness breaks in. When the oxen stumbled, Uzza reached out with a steadying hand, as anyone would. He meant to rescue what was falling; instead, he touched what he had no right to touch.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord's anger burned and Uzza fell dead on the instant. It is terrible and bewildering—a man's good intention becomes the occasion for God's judgment. There is something in God's holiness that says: even pity and goodwill cannot cross this line.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David's displeasure at God's breaking out against Uzza shows the human struggle: righteousness and fear together, love and recoil, joy turned to dread in an instant. He named the place Perez Uzza—'the breaking of Uzza'—to remember.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Fear seized David: 'How can I bring God's ark home to me?' This is a good fear—the beginning of wisdom, the recognition that holiness cannot be approached by human cleverness alone. When we draw near to the Lord, we must come by His way.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David stops the procession. He does not force the ark forward into his city but leaves it at Obed-Edom's house—a pause, a rest, a willingness to wait and learn. Surrender is not failure; sometimes the deepest obedience is knowing when to stop.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The ark remained three months, and the Lord blessed Obed-Edom's house. Readers today hear an echo in this: God's presence, resting with a humble servant, brings abundance where we least expect it. When we make room for the holy, even in a pause, blessing follows.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
